summary: Reviews the original function and purpose of the Domain Name System and contrasts it with newer uses and demands being placed on it. It outlines a framework for an alternative to loading those extra stresses onto DNS, offered as a strong suggestion rather than a proposed solution.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS was made to turn names into addresses, like a phone book. People started asking it to do much more. This note says maybe a different tool should do that extra work.

questions: what is the role of dns
should dns be used for directory services
what was dns originally designed for
what is a directory system alternative to dns
why is internationalization hard for dns
subtitle: Rethinking DNS as its original purpose overextends

tldr.problem: The Domain Name System was designed simply to translate names to IP addresses. Today it is overloaded with requests to also handle directories, multilingual names, content distribution, and trademark management.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews DNS's original design and constraints, then proposes a separate search or directory layer to handle new demands instead of patching DNS further.
tldr.outcome: Accepted as an informational document. The idea that DNS should remain focused on its original purpose has influenced thinking about protocol boundaries.

today: RFC 3467 remains an informational note. It has not been obsoleted, and its core insight—that DNS is being overloaded and that specialized alternatives may be more effective than patches—continues to influence discussion of Internet infrastructure and protocol boundaries.

sections.title: History and Original Design
sections.content:
The DNS replaced an earlier system called the host table, which was just a file listing hostnames and their network addresses. As the Internet grew, the DNS was created to do a few specific jobs: identify network resources uniquely, allow hierarchical organization of names, and scale by distributing administration across many sites. The designers knew this might be too limited in the future, so they made the protocol flexible enough to carry any data in its fields, not just addresses.

However, the actual DNS used in practice was restricted: hostnames could only use letters, digits and hyphens (the LDH rules), derived from avoiding ambiguities across different character sets and languages. The system assumed a deeply hierarchical structure where most names would represent actual physical hosts, not abstract concepts, people or products.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS started as a way to find computers by name instead of remembering numbers. It was built to grow through delegation, so many people could add their own names without a central office managing everything.

sections.title: When DNS Gets Overloaded
sections.content:
Over time, people have tried to press DNS into service for tasks it was never designed for. Some organizations want DNS to identify people or products as well as hosts. Others want one domain name to resolve to many different servers based on the user's location. The web's design choice to put DNS names directly in URLs created demand for short, memorable second-level domain names, flattening the DNS hierarchy. Some proposals would use DNS for full text search or fuzzy matching, neither of which the protocol supports. And internationalization efforts discovered that the LDH restrictions exclude most of the world's languages and scripts.

Each of these problems is real. Each has spun off workarounds and kludges — tricks like DNS name rewriting, special record types, and encoding schemes. But each workaround adds complexity and risk. The RFC argues that instead of continuing to patch DNS, we should recognize these are fundamentally different problems that deserve different solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS works fine for turning domain names into computer addresses. But people want it to also find products, brands, people, nearby servers, and translations. Adding all that makes DNS complicated and fragile.

sections.title: A Directory Layer Instead
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a directory or search layer as an alternative. A modern directory system like LDAP could sit between users and DNS, handling lookups that DNS cannot. This approach offers several advantages: a directory does not need to enforce worldwide uniqueness, can store multiple versions of a name (such as both romanized and native-script spellings), can return multiple results paired with location or context information, and can support fuzzy or phonetic matching rules adapted to local languages. If applications have to be modified to call a directory instead of DNS, they might as well call DNS afterward if needed.

The RFC emphasizes that this is not a quick fix: internationalization work in the IETF had taught the design group that the problems are far more subtle than simple encoding choices. But the suggestion is that a well-designed directory would be less painful than continuing to cram incompatible features into DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: A separate directory tool could handle fuzzy searches and different languages without forcing DNS to become something it was not built to be.

sections.title: The Multilingual Names Problem
sections.content:
One major driver of overload is the demand for domain names in scripts and languages other than English. The problem is more complex than picking a character set. Unicode provides multiple ways to represent the same character. Different languages have different case-folding rules, or no notion of case at all. Some scripts like Chinese can be written in Simplified or Traditional forms. Two names that look similar to speakers of one language might look identical to speakers of another, creating fraud risk. And when DNS was designed, it was never clear whether it should scale to represent individual users or products, rather than just network hosts.

The RFC notes that merely allowing non-ASCII characters in DNS would require changes to nearly every application that calls DNS, since they would need to accept input in multiple character sets. Once applications are being modified anyway, a switch to calling a directory service is a relatively small additional step.
sections.plainLanguage: Names in other languages have tricky rules: some letters can be written different ways, some pairs of letters look the same in one language but different in another. Trying to cram all that into DNS breaks things.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
The RFC notes that DNS uniqueness and universal accessibility are critical to Internet security and the end-to-end principle — the idea that the network should not change the meaning of names or hide their identity. A directory system that sits between the user and DNS would introduce new layers of trust and new opportunities for compromise. However, a well-designed directory could actually offer protections that pure DNS cannot: it could restrict access to sensitive information based on the requestor's credentials, and it could support different rules in different regions or for different communities without fragmenting the Internet as multiple DNS roots would.

The trade-off is that every new system and layer introduces some additional risk, but the RFC suggests those risks may be worth accepting if they allow each system to do its job well.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding a search tool between users and DNS means trusting another system, which is a security choice. But it might be safer than having DNS try to do everything at once.
